name: Fasted cardio
lead: Fasted cardio is aerobic exercise done after an overnight fast, usually first thing in the morning before eating. It is a staple of bodybuilding-style cutting phases, where practitioners believe that exercising with low carbohydrate stores shifts energy use toward body fat, helping them get leaner and more defined for a contest or a physique goal.[1][2] Leaner means visible muscle definition and, in the face, a sharper jawline, which is why it turns up in physique and looksmaxxing discussions.

On T Nation, members ask who is doing morning fasted cardio in cutting season, and one contest-prep log lists too much fasted cardio as a suspected cause of muscle loss, showing how lifters weigh it against keeping muscle.[3][4]

Controlled studies exist. A 2014 four-week trial in 20 young women on a calorie-restricted diet found both fasted and fed aerobic groups lost weight and fat mass with no significant between-group differences.[5] Later studies have looked at appetite, gut hormones, energy balance and fat distribution after fasted exercise.[6][7][8]

chain: Aerobic session after an overnight fast
Higher fat oxidation during the session
Added calorie burn toward a leaner, more defined physique
angle.text: Lifters add morning cardio before eating to their cutting phases to help reduce body fat so muscle and facial structure show more. The comparison trials that exist found similar fat loss whether training fasted or fed.

paras: In bodybuilding, competitors generally gain muscle in an off-season and then cut, eating below maintenance and adding cardiovascular exercise to lose fat before a contest.[1] Fasted cardio is a variant in which the session is done before any food that day, usually after sleep. A 2017 case report and critical review interviewed six competitive bodybuilders and their coaches about the nutrition, drug and training strategies used in bulking and cutting phases, and compared them with scientific evidence.[2]

Proponents say that with low liver glycogen and low insulin after an overnight fast, more fat is mobilized during exercise. Research supports a short-term shift in fuel use: in a 2019 study of 45-minute brisk walks in 12 men, blood non-esterified fatty acids were higher when fasted, while carbohydrate oxidation was greater when fed, and gastric emptying, appetite and acylated ghrelin did not differ.[6]

A 2024 paper notes that fasted exercise raises fat oxidation more than fed exercise in the short term, yet consistent fasted training usually does not produce extra weight loss, which the authors suggest may reflect compensation in energy balance.[7]

On T Nation, a poster in a 2021 transformation thread asks who is doing morning fasted cardio or conditioning and says the time of year seems to favour it.[3] In a contest prep log, a competitor lists too much fasted cardio, which he thinks probably led to muscle loss, among changes he would make, and notes his coach preferred low- and moderate-intensity cardio over HIIT in prep.[4]

Bodybuilding reports describe cardio as one of several levers used in a cut, alongside calorie intake and, for some competitors, drugs; the six-bodybuilder case report compares those practices with the research.[1][2]

Schoenfeld and colleagues randomized 20 young women on a calorie-restricted diet to fasted or fed aerobic training for four weeks, one hour three times per week; both groups lost significant weight and fat mass with no significant between-group differences.[5]

A 2019 study of 12 healthy men compared 45-minute brisk walks fasted versus fed and measured metabolic responses, gut function and appetite: fatty acid levels and carbohydrate oxidation differed as expected, while gastric emptying and appetite hormones did not.[6] A 2024 study of 12 active adults found fasted and fed 75-minute runs produced no differences in energy intake, total energy expenditure, appetite or glucose over four days, and the authors say both approaches could be used interchangeably.[7]

A 2025 pilot (the FED trial) in 20 adults with type 2 diabetes, 16 of whom completed it, compared 16 weeks of fasted versus postprandial morning walking. HbA1c did not change overall; after excluding two participants whose medication changed, the fasted group improved more (-0.3 percent versus 0.0). Liver fat changes did not differ, while visceral and intramuscular fat fell more after fasted exercise.[8]

The lifter reports in this record mention possible muscle loss with large amounts of fasted cardio, but no controlled study identified tests that claim directly.[4] Studies of fasted exercise in healthy and diabetic adults reported no safety problems in their summaries.[5][7][8]

lore.intro: Fasted cardio is discussed among lifters as a cutting tool and as something that might cost muscle if overdone [3][4].

claims.claim: Cardio on an empty stomach burns more fat and gets you leaner.
claims.believers: Lifters report using morning fasted cardio during cutting phases [3].
claims.experts: A four-week trial in women on a calorie-restricted diet found no significant difference in fat loss between fasted and fed cardio [5].

claims.claim: Too much fasted cardio can cost muscle.
claims.believers: A contest-prep log attributes probable muscle loss to excessive fasted cardio [4].
claims.experts: The fasted-versus-fed trials identified here did not report muscle outcomes in this way; no study has tested this claim directly.

claims.claim: Fasted cardio makes you hungrier, so you eat back the calories
claims.believers: Some lifters say empty-stomach sessions leave them with stronger appetite later in the day.
claims.experts: A 2024 four-day study found no difference in energy intake or appetite between fasted and fed runs, and a 2019 study found similar appetite hormones after fasted and fed walks.[6][7]

card.summary: Morning cardio before eating, a bodybuilding cutting habit with little direct research.
card.note: No controlled comparison of fasted and fed cardio has been published.

quick.overview:
Fasted cardio means doing aerobic exercise before the day's first meal. It is common in bodybuilding cuts.
No controlled trial compares it with fed cardio, so claims about added fat loss are untested.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say low carbohydrate availability after an overnight fast shifts fuel use toward fat during the session.
quick.risks: The one related paper is a case report on bodybuilders whose routines also included heavy anabolic steroid use.
